title: MLP generator lacks theoretical guarantees
description: Using a multilayer perceptron to define G introduces multiple critical points in parameter space, so adversarial nets lack theoretical guarantees despite their good practical performance.
canonical_description: multilayer perceptron parameterization introduces multiple critical points and lacks theoretical guarantees

evidence.anchor: introduces multiple critical points in parameter space
evidence.quote:
Using a multilayer perceptron to define $G$ introduces multiple
critical points in parameter space.

verdict.reasoning: Several papers supply partial theoretical grounding for adversarial/minimax training, but none addresses the gap's specific problem — that MLP parameterization of the generator introduces multiple critical points and thereby defeats theoretical guarantees. Paper 1 (Stackelberg dynamics) gives local convergence guarantees to differential Stackelberg equilibria for zero-sum games and connects them to GANs, but the guarantees are local, conditional on initialization, and rely on a realizable/zero-sum abstraction rather than analyzing MLP-induced critical points. Paper 2 gives tight local GDA convergence results for smooth nonconvex-nonconcave problems under local strong concavity and existence of a Stackelberg equilibrium, explicitly leaving the general nonconvex-nonconcave MLP setting open. Paper 3 (DRAGAN) restores local stability via discriminator smoothness/regularization, but not for plain MLP-parameterized GANs and without global or spurious-critical-point results. Paper 5 gives stationarity guarantees for two-timescale GDA only under nonconvex-concave structure, which excludes MLP-parameterized generators/discriminators. Paper 4 is not addressed, requiring Minty/structure assumptions unrelated to MLP parameterization. What remains open is exactly the core issue: a characterization of, or guarantee against, the multiple/spurious critical points induced by MLP parameterization, and any global convergence guarantee for plain MLP-parameterized adversarial nets.

paper.title: Convergence of Learning Dynamics in Stackelberg Games
paper.abstract: This paper investigates the convergence of learning dynamics in Stackelberg games. In the class of games we consider, there is a hierarchical game being played between a leader and a follower with continuous action spaces. We establish a number of connections between the Nash and Stackelberg equilibrium concepts and characterize conditions under which attracting critical points of simultaneous gradient descent are Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games. Moreover, we show that the only stable critical points of the Stackelberg gradient dynamics are Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games. Using this insight, we develop a gradient-based update for the leader while the follower employs a best response strategy for which each stable critical point is guaranteed to be a Stackelberg equilibrium in zero-sum games. As a result, the learning rule provably converges to a Stackelberg equilibria given an initialization in the region of attraction of a stable critical point. We then consider a follower employing a gradient-play update rule instead of a best response strategy and propose a two-timescale algorithm with similar asymptotic convergence guarantees. For this algorithm, we also provide finite-time high probability bounds for local convergence to a neighborhood of a stable Stackelberg equilibrium in general-sum games. Finally, we present extensive numerical results that validate our theory, provide insights into the optimization landscape of generative adversarial networks, and demonstrate that the learning dynamics we propose can effectively train generative adversarial networks.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper develops a convergence theory for hierarchical/Stackelberg learning dynamics in continuous general-sum games, proving that the only stable critical points of the Stackelberg gradient dynamics are differential Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games, and proposes two-timescale gradient-based algorithms (leader uses an implicit best-response gradient; follower uses gradient play) with asymptotic and finite-time high-probability local convergence guarantees. It explicitly connects these results to GANs (stable differential Nash ⇒ differential Stackelberg; necessary/sufficient conditions under the realizable assumption; examples showing non-Nash attractors of simultaneous gradient play can be Stackelberg equilibria) and empirically trains GANs with MLP generator/discriminator networks, arguing the stable attractors reached are meaningful equilibria. This supplies a form of theoretical guarantee for adversarial-type training that does not rely on convexity.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not analyze the specific source of the gap — the MLP parameterization of the generator introducing multiple critical points in parameter space. Its theory treats generic smooth games with arbitrary parameter action spaces; guarantees are local, i.e., convergence to a Stackelberg equilibrium only holds given initialization in the region of attraction of a stable critical point, and the characterization of which attractors are reached is not resolved globally. The GAN-specific theoretical statements require the realizable assumption and concern zero-sum abstractions, while the actual MLP-parameterized GAN training (DCGAN/MNIST, mixture of Gaussians) is validated empirically rather than covered by the theorems. Thus the open problem of providing theoretical guarantees for adversarial nets whose generator is an MLP — in the face of multiple/spurious critical points introduced by that parameterization — is only partially mitigated (via a reformulated Stackelberg learning rule with local guarantees), not solved.

paper.title: On Convergence of Gradient Descent Ascent: A Tight Local Analysis
paper.abstract: Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) methods are the mainstream algorithms for minimax optimization in generative adversarial networks (GANs). Convergence properties of GDA have drawn significant interest in the recent literature. Specifically, for $\min_{\mathbf{x}} \max_{\mathbf{y}} f(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y})$ where $f$ is strongly-concave in $\mathbf{y}$ and possibly nonconvex in $\mathbf{x}$, (Lin et al., 2020) proved the convergence of GDA with a stepsize ratio $η_{\mathbf{y}}/η_{\mathbf{x}}=Θ(κ^2)$ where $η_{\mathbf{x}}$ and $η_{\mathbf{y}}$ are the stepsizes for $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ and $κ$ is the condition number for $\mathbf{y}$. While this stepsize ratio suggests a slow training of the min player, practical GAN algorithms typically adopt similar stepsizes for both variables, indicating a wide gap between theoretical and empirical results. In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap by analyzing the \emph{local convergence} of general \emph{nonconvex-nonconcave} minimax problems. We demonstrate that a stepsize ratio of $Θ(κ)$ is necessary and sufficient for local convergence of GDA to a Stackelberg Equilibrium, where $κ$ is the local condition number for $\mathbf{y}$. We prove a nearly tight convergence rate with a matching lower bound. We further extend the convergence guarantees to stochastic GDA and extra-gradient methods (EG). Finally, we conduct several numerical experiments to support our theoretical findings.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper develops a tight local convergence analysis of two-timescale GDA (and its stochastic and extra-gradient variants) for smooth nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems, proving that a stepsize ratio r = Θ(κ) is necessary and sufficient for local convergence to a differential Stackelberg Equilibrium, with nearly matching convergence rates and lower bounds. It also runs GAN (WGAN-GP/DCGAN) experiments showing that simultaneous stepsizes converge in practice. This bears on the gap's "adversarial nets lack theoretical guarantees" concern by providing provable convergence guarantees for minimax training in a nonconvex regime that previously only had Θ(κ²) two-time-scale analyses.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is specifically about MLP parameterization of the generator introducing multiple critical points in parameter space and thereby preventing theoretical (global) guarantees for adversarial nets. This paper does not analyze the MLP/network-parameterization structure at all: it abstracts the generator and discriminator into a generic twice-differentiable objective f(x;y), assumes a differential Stackelberg Equilibrium already exists, assumes local smoothness and (local) strong concavity in y, and only establishes local convergence from a sufficiently close initialization (global guarantees are obtained only for quadratic NC-SC functions). It explicitly acknowledges that general nonconvex-nonconcave problems (where MLP-parameterized GANs live) remain intractable/unsettled. Hence the specific problem of multiple critical points introduced by MLP parameterization and global guarantees for MLP-parameterized adversarial nets is not resolved; what is added is only conditional, local convergence theory for an abstract smooth minimax formulation.
evidence_snippets: In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap by analyzing the \emph{local convergence} of general \emph{nonconvex-nonconcave} minimax problems. We demonstrate that a stepsize ratio of $\Theta(\kappa)$ is necessary and sufficient for local convergence of GDA to a Stackelberg Equilibrium
We further assume that there exists a differential Stackelberg Equilibrium $\vz^\ast=(\vx^\ast,\vy^\ast)$.
It remains an open problem how to define a nontrivial and tractable notion of minimax points.

paper.title: On Convergence and Stability of GANs
paper.abstract: We propose studying GAN training dynamics as regret minimization, which is in contrast to the popular view that there is consistent minimization of a divergence between real and generated distributions. We analyze the convergence of GAN training from this new point of view to understand why mode collapse happens. We hypothesize the existence of undesirable local equilibria in this non-convex game to be responsible for mode collapse. We observe that these local equilibria often exhibit sharp gradients of the discriminator function around some real data points. We demonstrate that these degenerate local equilibria can be avoided with a gradient penalty scheme called DRAGAN. We show that DRAGAN enables faster training, achieves improved stability with fewer mode collapses, and leads to generator networks with better modeling performance across a variety of architectures and objective functions.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper ("On Convergence and Stability of GANs", the DRAGAN paper) studies exactly the topic named by the gap: when and why GAN training converges or fails, and what theoretical conditions restore stability. It analyzes the adversarial game, shows that restricting the discriminator / enforcing smoothness (Lipschitz-type conditions via a gradient penalty near the data manifold, DRAGAN) leads the training dynamics toward local Nash equilibria / the true-data optimum, and provides an algorithm with improved stability. This bears directly on the gap's complaint that practical (MLP-parameterized) GANs lack theoretical grounding.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific claim is that MLP generator/discriminator parameterizations introduce multiple critical points in parameter space and therefore adversarial nets have no theoretical guarantees. The paper only partially closes this: its guarantees are local (convergence to local Nash equilibria) and are obtained under added assumptions/regularization (a smoothness/Lipschitz-type discriminator achieved by the proposed gradient penalty), not for the plain MLP minimax game. It does not prove that arbitrary MLP-parameterized GANs escape spurious critical points or converge to a global optimum, so the fundamental issue that MLP parameterization creates non-global critical points with no end-to-end guarantee remains. (Caveat: the supplied LaTeX body is only \includepdf[pages=1-last]{iclr_dragan.pdf}, so the paper's actual text was not available in this transcript for verbatim verification.)

paper.title: Semi-Anchored Multi-Step Gradient Descent Ascent Method for Structured Nonconvex-Nonconcave Composite Minimax Problems
paper.abstract: Minimax problems, such as generative adversarial network, adversarial training, and fair training, are widely solved by a multi-step gradient descent ascent (MGDA) method in practice. However, its convergence guarantee is limited. In this paper, inspired by the primal-dual hybrid gradient method, we propose a new semi-anchoring (SA) technique for the MGDA method. This makes the MGDA method find a stationary point of a structured nonconvex-nonconcave composite minimax problem; its saddle-subdifferential operator satisfies the weak Minty variational inequality condition. The resulting method, named SA-MGDA, is built upon a Bregman proximal point method. We further develop its backtracking line-search version, and its non-Euclidean version for smooth adaptable functions. Numerical experiments, including a fair classification training, are provided.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes a semi-anchored multi-step gradient descent ascent (SA-MGDA) method for structured nonconvex-nonconcave composite minimax problems whose saddle-subdifferential operator satisfies the weak (or strong) Minty variational inequality, proving O(1/k) and O(ε^{-1}log ε^{-1}) rates as well as backtracking line-search and non-Euclidean variants. This is an optimization-method paper about GAN-type minimax problems in general; it does not analyze the MLP parameterization of the generator G or the landscape it induces.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific gap — that an MLP parameterization of the generator introduces multiple critical points in parameter space, leaving adversarial nets without theoretical guarantees — is not addressed. The paper's convergence guarantees require structural assumptions that an MLP-generated objective need not satisfy: φ smooth with Lipschitz gradient, f and g closed proper convex (with f=g=0 or prox-friendly convex structure), weak/strong MVI on the saddle-subdifferential operator, and for the practical inexact version strong concavity/compactness of the inner maximization in v. Nothing is said about neural network (MLP) parameterization, about the nonconvex landscape in the network parameters, or about why training with such a G would avoid or be analyzed through spurious critical points. It also explicitly assumes an unconstrained composite form min_u max_v {f(u)+φ(u,v)-g(v)} rather than parameterizing G by an MLP, so the adversarial-net guarantee problem raised by the gap remains open.

paper.title: Two-Timescale Gradient Descent Ascent Algorithms for Nonconvex Minimax Optimization
paper.abstract: We provide a unified analysis of two-timescale gradient descent ascent (TTGDA) for solving structured nonconvex minimax optimization problems in the form of $\min_\textbf{x} \max_{\textbf{y} \in Y} f(\textbf{x}, \textbf{y})$, where the objective function $f(\textbf{x}, \textbf{y})$ is nonconvex in $\textbf{x}$ and concave in $\textbf{y}$, and the constraint set $Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is convex and bounded. In the convex-concave setting, the single-timescale gradient descent ascent (GDA) algorithm is widely used in applications and has been shown to have strong convergence guarantees. In more general settings, however, it can fail to converge. Our contribution is to design TTGDA algorithms that are effective beyond the convex-concave setting, efficiently finding a stationary point of the function $Φ(\cdot) := \max_{\textbf{y} \in Y} f(\cdot, \textbf{y})$. We also establish theoretical bounds on the complexity of solving both smooth and nonsmooth nonconvex-concave minimax optimization problems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of TTGDA for nonconvex minimax optimization, shedding light on its superior performance in training generative adversarial networks (GANs) and in other real-world application problems.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper provides nonasymptotic convergence guarantees for two-timescale gradient descent ascent (TTGDA/TTSGDA) algorithms on structured nonconvex-concave minimax problems min_x max_{y in Y} f(x,y), establishing gradient-evaluation complexity bounds to reach an ε-stationary point of Φ(x) = max_y f(x,y) in smooth and nonsmooth settings. Since TTGDA is the algorithm used empirically for training GANs, the paper supplies some theoretical backing (convergence to stationarity) for the "no guarantees" criticism of GAN training dynamics, and it explicitly frames its contribution as shedding light on GAN training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the gap's specific problem: guarantees for an MLP-parameterized generator. Its theory requires f(x, ·) to be concave in the maximization variable over a bounded convex set (nonconvex-concave structure), which excludes the standard GAN setup where both the generator and discriminator are MLPs and the loss is nonconvex-nonconcave; the paper even notes the fully nonconvex-nonconcave setting (the one created by MLP parameterization) is NP-hard and outside its scope. Moreover, its target is a local ε-stationary point of Φ (or an f-based stationarity notion), not the global saddle/equilibrium whose existence is threatened by the many critical points that MLP parameterization introduces. Consequently, the multiplicity of critical points induced by the MLP generator, the landscape structure, and which critical points TTGDA will actually converge to in real GANs remain unaddressed. Thus it solves part of the gap — providing convergence-to-stationarity guarantees for the algorithm class in a structured subcase — but only under limited assumptions, not for the MLP-generator setting the gap describes.

Imposing such one-side concavity is necessary since~[CITE:Daskalakis-2021-Complexity] have shown that it is NP-hard to determine if an approximate min-max point exists in a general smooth and nonconvex-nonconcave setting.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: This is a pure-theory gap, so data and compute are not the limiting factors. Feasibility is dominated by methodological difficulty: global convergence guarantees for nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems are a largely open problem, and the specific question of characterizing/avoiding spurious critical points introduced by MLP parameterization is close to the harder parts of deep-learning optimization theory. Existing results only give local or structure-restricted guarantees (local Stackelberg, nonconvex-concave, regularized discriminators), leaving the general MLP setting unresolved. The gap is also broad as stated—covering plain MLP-parameterized generators/discriminators and global behavior—rather than a narrow architecture or restricted training regime. Progress is measurable in principle via proved theorems, but a full solution likely requires a fundamental advance, not a routine extension of known tools. Focused sub-cases (e.g., shallow/overparameterized networks, strong regularization) could yield partial progress, but the core gap is low-to-moderate tractability.
